intro: Atoms of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water are never used up: they move between reservoirs (the air, living things, soil, rock, the ocean) by processes such as photosynthesis, nitrogen fixation and evaporation. Pick a cycle, tap a process to see what moves where and who does it, then switch on a human change and watch the reservoirs shift over the years.
howItWorks:
Carbon (in GtC, billion tonnes of carbon; amounts rounded from IPCC AR6 and the Global Carbon Project): the natural flows come in nearly balanced pairs. Human emissions are split as the recent global budget splits them: about 45% stays in the air, 25% dissolves in the ocean and 30% is taken up by land plants and soils. 1 ppm of atmospheric CO₂ is 2.12 GtC.

Nitrogen and phosphorus are shown as relative amounts (each reservoir starts at 100%) in a simple box model: every flow is proportional to the amount in its source, so a change spreads around the cycle. The nitrogen processes carry the order the exam uses: 1 fixation, 2 nitrification, 3 assimilation, 4 ammonification, 5 denitrification.

Water (in km³, rounded from Trenberth et al. 2007) uses the same box model. Paving cuts infiltration and raises runoff; pumping drains an aquifer; warming speeds evaporation and melts land ice.

The models show directions and rough sizes, not forecasts.
